newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid policemen left in lurch, says lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid policemen left in lurch, says lawyer.

text.p: The former policemen who killed renowned South African opposition leader Steve Biko in 1977 have been spurned by the apartheid masters they served, their lawyer said on Tuesday.

Lawyer Francois van der Merwe confirmed at a news conference that the five were in the process of seeking pardon from Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is authorised to grant amnesty for human rights violations during the war over apartheid.
"They could do with more support...they are virtual outcasts at this stage," Van der Merwe said.

At a news conference attended by the families of some of their victims, he appealed for understanding for the men who interrogated, tortured and killed a number of black opposition leaders, including Biko and at least nine others.
"My clients came forward with a concern to try to make a contribution to the work of the Truth Commission and to contribute to the process of reconciliation," he said.

Van der Merwe said many of the policemen had never told their families about their work during the apartheid years and were having to explain to their wives and children why they killed men who had become heroes of South Africa's first democracy.
Joyce Mtimkulu, whose son Siphiwe was tortured, drugged, shot in the head and burned by South African security police said after the news conference: "I will never forgive them."
Monica Godolozi, whose husband was killed and burned in a separate incident, said the plight of the perpetrators' families was not her concern.
"I am not happy today. I have heard new information about how they treated my husband," she said.

Van der Merwe identified his clients, aged up to 75, as Colonel Harold Snyman, Lieutenant Colonel Gideon Niewoudt, Warrant Officer Ruben Marx, Captain Daantjie Siebert and Warrant Officer Johan Beneke.
He said some had been forced to seek amnesty after they were named in TRC hearings intended to unravel the human rights history of apartheid. Others had come forward of their own accord.
"They acted in the belief that they were acting to protect a system," he said of the crimes committed in the name of apartheid.

Van der Merwe said that not all cases of assault coming before the commission were authorised by the former government. "A lot of incidents were dealt with at lower levels but within the culture of the government of the day.
"In many of these instances, there is not a direct link right to the top...but there is a chain of command."
Truth commission deputy chairman Alex Boraine said earlier that no evidence had come in yet linking the tendered confessions of the five to politicians or generals.
